message.content:
In computer‑vision pipelines, “purple” isn’t a special semantic concept on its own—it’s just one of many RGB values that can be used to encode information.  In practice, purple is most commonly seen in two contexts:

1. **Label/Mask Encoding**  
   When creating ground‑truth masks for semantic or instance segmentation, each class is assigned a distinct RGB triplet so that the mask can be visualised and later decoded back into class IDs.  Purple (e.g., RGB (128, 0, 128) or similar) is often chosen simply because it is visually distinct from other common class colours (red, green, blue, yellow, etc.).  In such a mask, all pixels labelled with that purple value would correspond to the same object class.

2. **Annotation / Highlighting**  
   In annotation tools or post‑processing visualisations, purple is sometimes used as a highlight colour to draw attention to a region of interest, a bounding box, or a keypoint.  Because it stands out against typical natural‑scene backgrounds, it is useful for debugging or presentation purposes.

Beyond those uses, purple has no inherent meaning in computer‑vision algorithms; it is treated like any other colour channel value unless you explicitly map it to a semantic class or use it as a visual cue.
